title: Developing others in uncertainty
author: Dr Haili Hughes
summary: Written from inside her own upheaval - emigrating to Australia while responsible for the professional learning of nearly a thousand staff - Hughes argues that when the climate is uncertain, leaders reflexively push performance, and development stalls as a result. Her counter-proposal has five parts: cut cognitive load rather than ambition, develop people through sense-making rather than instruction, let change move slowly enough to become practice, protect dignity as the hidden engine of growth, and build ladders rather than cliffs. She leans on Sweller on cognitive load, Weick on sensemaking, Edmondson on psychological safety and Ryan and Deci on self-determination, but the argument stays concrete: if a priority cannot be seen in a classroom in under thirty seconds, it is a slogan rather than a practice. The essay's sharpest observation is that threatened dignity produces camouflage - beautifully formatted plans and tense staff - which looks like performance and is not growth. It ends on retention, reframing departures not as weakness but as a verdict on a future that looks like more of the same forever. The test she leaves leaders is whether staff, looking back in three years, would have evidence that this period helped them grow rather than merely endure.
points: Hughes replaces 'roll-outs' with 'meaning-making' in PD, anchored by three questions: what problem are we solving, what will change in lessons, and what evidence tells us it is working.
Her thirty-second test for a priority - can it be seen in a classroom that fast - is a cheap filter for distinguishing implementable priorities from slogans.
The claim that constant rapid change triggers chronic stress, which degrades cognition, which makes teaching harder, frames workload as a learning problem rather than a morale problem.
The ladder-not-cliff framing asks leaders to name one behaviour routine, one explanation technique and one questioning move rather than expecting fluency to follow from awareness.
A compelling future, she argues, is not a slogan but three felt experiences - continuity, agency and growth - and retention fractures when all three are absent.
quotes: In that kind of climate, leaders often feel pressure to crank the dial to maximum performance. The trouble is: when we push performance without attending to security and growth, development doesn’t accelerate - it stalls.
There’s a leadership lie that sounds noble but behaves like a cursed object: “We can do it all.” The reality is closer to: “We can do it all… badly… while developing a twitch.
Clarity is kindness. Confusion is expensive. Confusion costs time, morale, and that invisible resource called teacher brain.

In uncertainty, instruction is tempting. It feels decisive: “Here’s what we’re doing.” But when people don’t understand the why, they comply until the next email and then they quietly revert, because the change never became theirs.
If you want a change to stick, it must survive Tuesday Period 5, in February, with the class that thinks your instructions are optional. That takes practice, not a poster.
Most school systems accidentally build cliffs. We expect staff to leap from knowing about a practice to doing it fluently under pressure. That’s not development, it’s wishful thinking with a lanyard.
In uncertain times, people don’t need leaders with all the answers. They need leaders who help them grow, make sense of complexity and believe there is a future worth investing in.
